claims.text: The as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloy is initially an ordered single-phase hexagonal material.
The as-deposited baseline has a homogeneous microstructure.
A spatial substrate-temperature gradient during physical vapor deposition can create spatially varying microstructure.
The deposition gradient can vary local grain size, grain-boundary density, or defect distribution.
The microstructural gradient can be introduced while retaining the single-phase hexagonal structure.
Variations in grain size, boundary density, or defects produce a distribution of local nucleation barriers for the first-order magnetostructural transformation.
A distribution of local nucleation barriers makes the magnetostructural transition more gradual and spreads it over a wider temperature range.
Transition broadening reduces the sharp magnetic-entropy jump.
Transition broadening reduces hysteretic losses during low-field magnetic cycling.
The engineered microstructure increases phase-boundary density.
Increased phase-boundary density improves heat exchange.
Gradient-deposited samples will have a broader magnetocaloric response than uniformly deposited controls.
Gradient-deposited samples will have lower magnetic-cycle hysteresis than uniformly deposited controls.
Gradient-deposited samples will exchange heat more effectively than uniformly deposited controls.
The predicted effects apply only when secondary phases are avoided and the initial single-phase hexagonal structure is preserved.
The predicted effects apply in the low-applied-field regime relevant to practical refrigeration cycles.
Uniform-temperature and spatially gradient-temperature films should be compared under otherwise matched deposition and low-field cycling conditions.
Failure of gradient films to show transition broadening, hysteresis reduction, or improved heat exchange relative to the control would falsify the proposed explanation.
